title: Limits and continuity
summary: What a function approaches, and whether it jumps.

layers.basics: A limit asks what value a function heads toward as its input nears some point. A function is continuous if you can draw it without lifting the pen.
layers.deeper: Limits make instantaneous change and infinite sums precise. Circuit voltages across a capacitor are continuous; a switch flipping is modelled as a jump that the capacitor smooths.
layers.expert: ε–δ definition: for every ε>0 there is δ>0 with |x−a|<δ ⇒ |f(x)−L|<ε. Piecewise models (ideal switches, step inputs) are discontinuous; physical energy storage keeps state variables continuous.

title: Derivative
summary: The instantaneous rate of change of a quantity.

layers.basics: The derivative tells how fast something is changing right now: speed from position, current from charge.
layers.deeper: Rules for sums, products, chains and common functions turn rate-of-change questions into algebra. In circuits, i = C·dv/dt and v = L·di/dt are derivatives.
layers.expert: f′(x)=lim h→0 [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h. Linearization f(x+δ)≈f(x)+f′(x)δ underlies small-signal models of every nonlinear device.

title: Integral and the fundamental theorem
summary: Accumulating a rate over time or space.

layers.basics: An integral adds up many tiny pieces: total charge from current over time, or total energy from power.
layers.deeper: The fundamental theorem links differentiation and integration as inverse operations, so antiderivatives compute areas exactly.
layers.expert: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = F(b)−F(a). Capacitor voltage v(t)=v(0)+(1/C)∫i dt; energy E=∫p dt. Riemann and Lebesgue definitions agree on well-behaved signals.

formula: Q = ∫ i dt;  E = ∫ p dt

title: Techniques of integration
summary: Substitution, parts, partial fractions.

layers.basics: Tricks to evaluate integrals that do not look simple: substitute a new variable, split into pieces, or use parts.
layers.deeper: Partial fractions are especially important because they invert Laplace and z transforms of rational functions.
layers.expert: Integration by parts ∫u dv=uv−∫v du; improper integrals converge or diverge by comparison tests; numerical quadrature takes over when no closed form exists.

title: Sequences and infinite series
summary: Adding infinitely many terms and when it settles.

layers.basics: A series adds endless terms; some, like 1+½+¼+…, add up to a finite number.
layers.deeper: Convergence tests (ratio, comparison, integral) decide whether the sum exists. Geometric series appear in transmission-line multiple reflections and in the z-transform.
layers.expert: Σ rⁿ = 1/(1−r) for |r|<1. Absolute vs conditional convergence matters when rearranging terms; uniform convergence justifies termwise differentiation.

title: Taylor and power series
summary: Approximating a function by a polynomial.

layers.basics: Near a point, almost any smooth function looks like a polynomial; more terms give a better match.
layers.deeper: Engineers truncate Taylor series to linearize a transistor curve or to derive sin x ≈ x for small angles; e^x and sin/cos are exactly their series.
layers.expert: f(x)=Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x−a)ⁿ/n!. Remainder bounds quantify truncation error. Radius of convergence is set by the nearest complex singularity.

title: Vectors, dot and cross product
summary: Quantities with magnitude and direction.

layers.basics: Vectors describe forces and fields. The dot product measures alignment; the cross product gives a perpendicular vector.
layers.deeper: Components in Cartesian, cylindrical and spherical coordinates let fields be written for the geometry at hand.
layers.expert: a·b=|a||b|cosθ, a×b=|a||b|sinθ n̂. Orthogonal curvilinear coordinates carry scale factors that enter gradient, divergence and curl.

title: Partial derivatives
summary: Rates of change with several variables.

layers.basics: When a quantity depends on many inputs, a partial derivative asks how it changes if only one input moves.
layers.deeper: Partials give the slope of a transistor current with respect to gate voltage while drain voltage is held fixed: the transconductance.
layers.expert: Total differential df=Σ(∂f/∂xᵢ)dxᵢ; the Jacobian generalises the chain rule and drives small-signal linearization and Newton iteration.

title: Gradient and directional derivative
summary: The direction of steepest increase.

layers.basics: The gradient points uphill. Electric field is the downhill direction of potential: E = −∇V.
layers.deeper: It turns a scalar map (potential, temperature) into a vector field and is perpendicular to level surfaces.
layers.expert: ∇f=(∂f/∂x,∂f/∂y,∂f/∂z); directional derivative D_u f=∇f·u. Gradient descent for optimization and training uses the same object.

title: Multiple integrals
summary: Integrating over areas and volumes.

layers.basics: Double and triple integrals add up a quantity over a surface or a volume, such as total charge from a charge density.
layers.deeper: Polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates make symmetric problems easy, with a Jacobian factor for the volume element.
layers.expert: Fubini lets iterated integrals swap order; change of variables multiplies by |det J|. Q=∭ρ dV is the source integral for Gauss’s law.

title: Vector fields and line integrals
summary: Fields and work done along a path.

layers.basics: A vector field assigns an arrow to every point. A line integral adds the field’s push along a path, like work or voltage.
layers.deeper: If the field is conservative the answer depends only on endpoints, which is why voltage between two nodes is well defined in a static circuit.
layers.expert: ∫C F·dr; F=∇φ iff curl F=0 on simply connected domains. Faraday induction breaks conservativeness, which is why KVL needs care with changing flux.

title: Divergence and curl
summary: How a field spreads out and how it swirls.

layers.basics: Divergence is net outflow per unit volume (sources and sinks); curl measures local rotation.
layers.deeper: Two of Maxwell’s equations are statements about divergence and two about curl.
layers.expert: ∇·F=∂Fx/∂x+∂Fy/∂y+∂Fz/∂z; ∇×F is the circulation density. Identities: ∇×∇φ=0, ∇·(∇×F)=0.

title: Green’s theorem
summary: Circulation around a loop equals curl inside.

layers.basics: A loop integral around a flat region equals the total swirl inside it.
layers.deeper: It is the 2-D case of Stokes’ theorem and the first bridge between local differential and global integral forms.
layers.expert: ∮(P dx+Q dy)=∬(∂Q/∂x−∂P/∂y)dA for positively oriented piecewise-smooth boundaries.

title: Stokes’ theorem
summary: Circulation around an edge equals flux of curl through a surface.

layers.basics: The line integral of a field around a closed loop equals the flux of its curl through any surface bounded by that loop.
layers.deeper: Turns Faraday’s law from differential to integral form: EMF around a loop equals −dΦ/dt.
layers.expert: ∮∂S F·dr=∬S(∇×F)·dS. Independence of surface follows from ∇·(∇×F)=0.

title: Divergence theorem
summary: Net outflow through a closed surface equals source inside.

layers.basics: Add up all the sources inside a volume and you get the total flow leaving through its surface.
layers.deeper: It converts Gauss’s law between its integral and point forms and gives charge conservation.
layers.expert: ∯S F·dS=∭V(∇·F)dV. Applied to J: ∇·J=−∂ρ/∂t.

title: First-order ODEs
summary: Equations linking a quantity to its own rate.

layers.basics: First-order equations, like dv/dt = −v/RC, describe exponential approach to a final value: charging, cooling, decay.
layers.deeper: Separable and linear first-order equations have closed forms; the integrating factor handles driven cases.
layers.expert: y′+p(t)y=q(t) has y=e^{−∫p}[∫q e^{∫p}dt+C]. Time constant τ sets 63% rise in 1τ and ~99% in 5τ.

title: Second-order linear ODEs
summary: Oscillation, damping and resonance.

layers.basics: Second-order equations govern masses on springs and RLC circuits: they can ring, decay smoothly, or in between.
layers.deeper: The characteristic equation s²+2ζω₀s+ω₀²=0 has real, repeated or complex roots giving over-, critical or under-damping.
layers.expert: General solution = homogeneous + particular. Undetermined coefficients or variation of parameters handle drives; Q=1/(2ζ).

title: Systems of ODEs
summary: Many coupled quantities evolving together.

layers.basics: Multi-capacitor and multi-inductor circuits give several linked equations, written as one matrix equation.
layers.deeper: Eigenvalues of the system matrix are the circuit’s natural frequencies; eigenvectors are its modes.
layers.expert: ẋ=Ax+Bu with x(t)=e^{At}x₀+∫e^{A(t−τ)}Bu dτ. This is state-space form, shared by circuits, mechanics and control.

title: Laplace transform
summary: Turning differential equations into algebra.

layers.basics: The Laplace transform converts calculus problems about time into algebra in a new variable s, then converts back.
layers.deeper: Derivatives become multiplication by s, so a circuit ODE becomes an algebraic equation, with initial conditions built in.
layers.expert: F(s)=∫₀^∞ f(t)e^{−st}dt; L{f′}=sF−f(0); final-value and initial-value theorems; inverse via partial fractions or the Bromwich integral.

title: Introduction to PDEs
summary: Heat, wave and Laplace equations.

layers.basics: Partial differential equations describe fields varying in space and time: heat flow, waves on a line, and voltage on a conductor.
layers.deeper: Separation of variables splits a PDE into ODEs. The wave equation underlies transmission lines; Laplace’s equation underlies electrostatics.
layers.expert: Heat: u_t=αu_xx; wave: u_tt=c²u_xx; Laplace: ∇²φ=0. Boundary conditions and uniqueness theorems decide which solutions are physical; numerical solvers (FDM, FEM) fill in for awkward geometries.

title: Matrices and linear systems
summary: Rectangular arrays that solve many equations at once.

layers.basics: A matrix stores a list of equations compactly. Gaussian elimination solves them step by step.
layers.deeper: Nodal and mesh analysis of any circuit reduces to Ax=b with a conductance or impedance matrix.
layers.expert: LU factorization costs ~⅔n³ flops; ill-conditioned A amplifies error by condition number κ(A). Sparse solvers power circuit simulators.

title: Determinants
summary: A single number telling if a matrix is invertible.

layers.basics: The determinant is zero exactly when the equations are dependent, so there is no unique solution.
layers.deeper: It measures volume scaling of the transformation and appears in Cramer’s rule and in characteristic polynomials.
layers.expert: det(AB)=det A·det B; det A=Πλᵢ. Singular node-admittance matrices flag floating nodes in a circuit.

title: Vector spaces and bases
summary: Sets where you can add and scale; choosing coordinates.

layers.basics: A vector space is any collection you can add and scale, from arrows to signals. A basis is a set of building blocks.
layers.deeper: Fourier series treat signals as vectors in a space whose basis is sines and cosines; inner products give projections.
layers.expert: Span, independence, dimension, rank-nullity; orthogonal projection onto a subspace gives least squares; Hilbert spaces extend to infinite dimension.

title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
summary: Directions that a matrix only stretches.

layers.basics: An eigenvector is not turned by a matrix, only scaled by its eigenvalue.
layers.deeper: Eigenvalues are the natural frequencies and decay rates of linear systems and decide stability.
layers.expert: Av=λv, det(A−λI)=0. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors; the spectrum of A_state places closed-loop poles.

title: Matrix decompositions (LU, QR, SVD)
summary: Factoring matrices for stable computation and insight.

layers.basics: Breaking a matrix into simpler pieces makes solving, compressing and analysing data easier.
layers.deeper: SVD finds the dominant patterns in data (principal components, noise removal); QR gives stable least squares; Cholesky speeds symmetric solves.
layers.expert: A=UΣVᵀ with singular values σ₁≥σ₂≥…; truncated SVD is the best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young). Used in MIMO precoding, Kalman filter square-root forms and balanced model reduction.

title: Random variables and distributions
summary: Numbers whose values come with probabilities.

layers.basics: A random variable assigns a number to an uncertain outcome. Its distribution says how likely each value is.
layers.deeper: Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, uniform, exponential and Gaussian distributions model bit errors, packet arrivals, component lifetimes and noise.
layers.expert: PMF/PDF/CDF; the Gaussian N(μ,σ²) emerges from sums by the central limit theorem, which is why thermal noise is Gaussian.

title: Expectation and variance
summary: Average value and spread.

layers.basics: The expected value is the long-run average; variance measures how widely values scatter around it.
layers.deeper: Noise power is variance; signal-to-noise ratio is a ratio of expectations.
layers.expert: E[X]=∫x f dx; Var X=E[X²]−E[X]²; covariance and correlation generalise to pairs; linearity of expectation holds without independence.

title: Random processes
summary: Signals that evolve randomly in time.

layers.basics: A random process is a whole family of possible waveforms, like all the possible noise traces from a resistor.
layers.deeper: Stationarity lets us describe a process by its autocorrelation and power spectral density.
layers.expert: Wiener–Khinchin: S(f)=F{R(τ)}. White noise has flat PSD; filtering by H(f) multiplies PSD by |H(f)|². Ergodicity lets one long trace stand in for the ensemble.

title: Noise modelling
summary: Thermal, shot and flicker noise.

layers.basics: Every resistor hisses faintly from random electron motion; every current also carries shot noise from discrete charges.
layers.deeper: Thermal noise 4kTRB, shot noise 2qIB and 1/f noise are modelled as random sources added to circuits.
layers.expert: v_n²=4kTRΔf (Johnson–Nyquist); noise figure F=SNR_in/SNR_out; Friis cascade sets receiver sensitivity. Quantum limits appear at very low T or high f.

title: Estimation
summary: Inferring hidden values from noisy data.

layers.basics: Estimation turns noisy measurements into the best guess of the underlying quantity.
layers.deeper: Least squares, maximum likelihood, and Kalman filtering are the working tools of sensors, GPS and radar.
layers.expert: Cramér–Rao bound Var(θ̂)≥1/I(θ). Kalman filter is the MMSE estimator for linear-Gaussian state-space models; Bayesian estimation gives the posterior.

title: Complex numbers
summary: Numbers with a real and an imaginary part.

layers.basics: Complex numbers a+jb live on a plane; engineers write j so as not to confuse it with current i.
layers.deeper: Multiplying by j rotates by 90°. Magnitude and phase make sinusoids easy to add.
layers.expert: Polar form re^{jθ}; conjugate z*; |z|²=zz*; the complex plane is the natural home of impedances, poles and spectra.

title: Euler’s formula
summary: e^{jθ} = cosθ + j sinθ.

layers.basics: Euler’s formula ties exponentials to sines and cosines and turns trigonometry into multiplication.
layers.deeper: Proven by comparing Taylor series. cosωt = Re{e^{jωt}} is the basis of phasors.
layers.expert: cosθ=(e^{jθ}+e^{−jθ})/2; Euler identity e^{jπ}=−1; generalises to complex exponentials as eigenfunctions of LTI systems.

title: Phasors
summary: Rotating arrows that stand in for sinusoids.

layers.basics: A phasor captures the size and phase of a sinusoid at a known frequency, so adding waves means adding arrows.
layers.deeper: Differentiation becomes multiplication by jω, which is why AC circuits behave like algebraic DC ones.
layers.expert: v(t)=Re{V e^{jωt}} with V=|V|∠φ. Valid for steady-state linear systems at a single frequency; superpose across frequencies.

title: Poles, zeros and the s-plane
summary: Where a transfer function blows up or vanishes.

layers.basics: Poles are the complex frequencies where a system’s response is infinite, zeros where it vanishes. Together they sketch the response.
layers.deeper: Poles in the left half-plane mean decaying behaviour (stable); on the imaginary axis, oscillation; in the right half, runaway.
layers.expert: H(s)=K Π(s−zᵢ)/Π(s−pⱼ). Frequency response is |H(jω)| read off the pole-zero plot by distances to jω.

title: Contour integration basics
summary: Integrals in the complex plane via residues.

layers.basics: Integrals along loops in the complex plane can be computed from the poles inside them.
layers.deeper: It gives inverse Laplace transforms and some real integrals that otherwise resist; also the Nyquist stability criterion’s argument principle.
layers.expert: ∮f dz=2πj Σ Res f(zₖ) (Cauchy). Argument principle: N=Z−P encirclements. Jordan’s lemma handles semicircle arcs.

title: Logic, sets and Boolean algebra
summary: Reasoning with true/false and collections.

layers.basics: Logic combines true/false statements with AND, OR and NOT; sets collect things; Boolean algebra is the algebra of both.
layers.deeper: Boolean algebra is exactly what logic gates compute; De Morgan’s laws let you swap AND and OR.
layers.expert: Boolean lattice axioms; De Morgan: ¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B. Shannon (1937) showed relay circuits implement Boolean algebra.

title: Graphs and trees
summary: Nodes and edges.

layers.basics: A graph is dots joined by lines. A circuit diagram is a graph, and so is a network of computers.
layers.deeper: Trees and cut sets give systematic mesh and node counts; shortest-path algorithms route packets.
layers.expert: Kirchhoff’s matrix-tree theorem counts spanning trees from the Laplacian; independent KCL equations = n−1, KVL = b−n+1.

title: Combinatorics
summary: Counting arrangements.

layers.basics: Permutations and combinations count the ways things can be ordered or chosen.
layers.deeper: Used to count code words, bit patterns and error events, and in probability.
layers.expert: C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n−k)!); binomial pmf P(k errors)=C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)^{n−k}; the number of binary words of length n is 2ⁿ.

title: Numerical root finding
summary: Solving f(x)=0 by iteration.

layers.basics: When an equation cannot be solved on paper, step toward the answer by repeated guesses (bisection, Newton).
layers.deeper: Circuit simulators solve nonlinear diode and transistor equations with Newton–Raphson at every timestep.
layers.expert: xₙ₊₁=xₙ−f/f′ converges quadratically near simple roots; bisection is slow but sure; damping and homotopy help SPICE convergence.

title: Numerical integration
summary: Approximating areas by sums.

layers.basics: Trapezoid and Simpson rules estimate integrals from sampled values.
layers.deeper: Used inside simulators to step through time and to compute energy and RMS from measured data.
layers.expert: Trapezoid error O(h²), Simpson O(h⁴); Gauss quadrature reaches higher order with fewer points.

title: Numerical ODE solvers
summary: Stepping differential equations forward in time.

layers.basics: Euler’s method advances using the slope; better methods (Runge–Kutta, backward Euler) are more accurate or more stable.
layers.deeper: SPICE uses implicit trapezoidal or Gear methods so that stiff circuits with fast and slow time constants stay stable.
layers.expert: Local error O(hᵖ⁺¹); stiffness requires A-stable implicit methods; adaptive step control keeps error below tolerance.

title: Error analysis
summary: Rounding, truncation, and conditioning.

layers.basics: Every computation and measurement has error; knowing how big it is makes results trustworthy.
layers.deeper: Truncation error from approximating, round-off from finite digits, and conditioning that amplifies both.
layers.expert: Machine epsilon 2⁻⁵² for doubles; catastrophic cancellation; propagation δf≈Σ|∂f/∂xᵢ|δxᵢ; backward stability.

title: Fourier analysis (mathematical view)
summary: Any signal is a sum of sinusoids.

layers.basics: Fourier showed that periodic waves are sums of sine waves at multiples of a base frequency.
layers.deeper: Orthogonality of sines makes the coefficients easy to compute with an integral; the idea extends to non-repeating signals.
layers.expert: Convergence (Dirichlet), Gibbs overshoot ~9% at jumps, Parseval’s theorem equates energy in time and frequency.
